I don't recommend this. Faking happiness really doesn't get people to like you. It makes you more tolerable on a superficial level of interaction, but can actually do damage when attempting to form real relationships.

As for your problem, some people might be waiting for you to give more of yourself to them, to show some vulnerability. Sharing problems isn't usually about finding solutions. It's about finding things in common and building social rapport. 

A normal person complaining about their problems is not the same as a lonely person wanting to share more of themselves. The two types of people have completely different understandings of very similar behavior.

Not trying to put you down man! I wasn't sure if it was a stylistic choice or not. It's difficult to give advice like this, because I don't want to stomp out anything unique in your writing that might become something great later on, but I'll just give one example. Mind you, this is a very subjective sort of critique. 

> Langden continued to tread down the road, until he came across a bridge. 

Immediately, you give us a character and sense of space. Awesome.

> He could only see because of the frequent lamp posts evenly spread on the path.

A common alternative would be to imply that the reader is already knows we're viewing this scene from your protagonist's perspective. This makes "He could only see" a bit redundant, unless there is something specifically unique about your character's sense of sight.

Often times once the reader is in your protagonist's point of view, you can just go on with descriptions and assume your reader will know who it's coming from. If you used, "Lanterns, evenly spaced, were the only road's source of light." We would know Langen is seeing this. He's the only character in the scene so far! 

An alternative is to move the pronoun to add superior mental imagery. Here's a couple lines from the intro of a Sanderson novel:

"Wax peeked up over the knotted boards, scanning the empty town. **Blue lines hovered in his vision,** extending from his chest to point at nearby sources of metal, a result of his Allomancy."

He doesn't say, "He could see blue lines..." Instead he turns the visuals into the subject. 

I don't think there's anything wrong about pronoun subject use, in fact Sanderson does that exact thing in The Alloy of Law's first paragraph, but the repetitious use of it can wear your reader out.

I was arrested in a Middle Eastern country after someone accused me of insulting the monarch. The accuser was a local nomad at a famous archaeological site who ran scams on naive tourists. Earlier that day I had interfered with his racket, preventing a confused Japanese girl from handing over 30 local currency units.

I returned to my hostel at 9:00 p.m. and found him and his friends waiting outside, smoking shisha. We shouted back and forth a few times. I ended up in tourist police custody.

The tourist police held me for 8 hours. They interrogated me slowly in broken English, and at random intervals burst out with "DID YOU INSULT THE KING?!" I told them I didn't. Then they transferred me to the real police station. I was to stay there for an indeterminate period of time, until the governor of the area had a chance to meet me and decide my legal fate. Which was probably not good, since I had pleaded the fifth (right to remain silent) half the time. But the Kingdom cares little for the US constitution.

Fortunately I was released around 4 in the morning after a high-ranking officer strolled in, shrugged his shoulders, and told them to let me go.

The cop who arrested me gave me a half-eaten stem of grapes and drove me to the center of the sleeping town as a dust-storm rolled in.

The story goes on from there, and there were a lot of details I left out. I plan on writing a book about my experiences one day.
